body: The cars are three deep at the barrier of a church compound in a Gulf city before seven on a Friday morning, engines running, air conditioning on in all of them. One man is early because he is always early. Inside, the previous service is still going and will not be out for another quarter of an hour, so the men from his congregation stand about in the car park in the flat early light, holding takeaway coffee, talking about nothing. When the doors open a Filipino congregation comes out of one hall and an Indian congregation goes into another, and his own service begins in the third, in Arabic, at seven exactly, because at eight another one needs the room.

There are people who would find that scene surprising, and the surprise is the subject of this article. Nothing in that car park was new, unusual, or the result of anybody’s campaign. It was a Friday.
For most Western listeners Arabic arrives pre-loaded with a single association, and the idea of Christian worship in it registers either as a novelty or as a missionary tactic. It is neither.

Take the word worship literally for a moment, because it is where the confusion sits. Worship is not a genre and it is not a repertoire; it is what a community does when it gathers, in whatever language that community happens to speak at home. Arab Christians are named at Pentecost, in the list of who heard. There were Arab bishops sitting at early councils and Arab tribes whose Christianity is a matter of record long before the seventh century. Their books and their formal liturgies were often in Syriac or in Greek — as the learned books of Europe were in Latin for a very long time — but the language in the mouths of the people standing in the room was the language they used in the market and at home. Arab Christians were praying in Arabic centuries before the seventh century, and have never stopped.

The band gives that continuity a permanent number. HM 328.70 — Inspire Crown — is the Arabic-language station, one of 40 international frequencies on a dial that runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70, and it is on air now.

Holding a number like that costs more than it looks. A frequency assigned to a language is a frequency that cannot be reassigned later to something with a wider audience, and a station in a language whose Christians are a minority is never going to be the argument anybody makes to a sponsor. It is also work that has to be done from inside — presenters who speak it as a first language, a catalogue written in it rather than rendered into it, and a schedule that assumes the listener already knows what the songs are about. The expensive form of respect is to give a church a frequency of its own and then keep it there.

The reason this is even necessary is a habit of mind rather than an argument. Languages acquire single associations in the public imagination, and once the association sets, everything else that the language has ever carried becomes invisible. Arabic in particular arrives in most Western ears already attached to one thing, and the effect on Arab Christians is that they are constantly being introduced to their own inheritance. They get asked when they converted. They get complimented on their English and asked how they came to the faith, by people who assume there was a moment, in a family where there has not been a moment for as far back as anyone can trace.

One consequence is worth stating plainly, because it catches people out. Arabic-speaking Christians use the ordinary Arabic word for God, and they use it for the simple reason that it is the ordinary Arabic word for God and always has been. It stands in Arabic Bibles and it stands in Arabic liturgy. Arab Christians have never needed anybody’s permission to say it, and they are not borrowing it from anyone.
Which is where broadcasting stops being a nice idea and becomes the practical question.

The alternative model is outreach, and it deserves a fair hearing, because outreach broadcasting has done real good for a century and the people who built it were serious. But an outreach signal has a shape you can hear in about four minutes. It explains. It assumes the listener is outside and is being invited in. It introduces the faith as something arriving, defines its terms, and pitches every hour at somebody who has not heard. Aim that at a church that has been in the region since before the region was arranged into its present countries, and the effect is not offence exactly. It is a slow, constant misfiling — a signal that keeps addressing a stranger while the actual listener sits there being told about their own house.
A station is not the same thing as a broadcast aimed at somebody.

A nurse comes off a late shift in Sheffield and sits in her car on the third floor of the multi-storey for a minute before starting it, because the shift was long. She puts the station on and it comes up mid-song. A colleague she has agreed to drop at the station gets in, listens for a while, and says she had assumed it was something from a mosque. The nurse says it is a hymn about the resurrection, and that her grandmother sang it in Alexandria. The colleague says nothing for a bit, then says she likes it, and then they talk about the parking charges the whole way down the ramp, and the hymn is still playing when they get to the barrier.
That is the whole mechanism, and it did not require a single explanatory sentence. The song went first and the correction happened by itself.

Now the honest part. Naming this history does not make it comfortable. Arab Christians have paid for it, and are paying — communities that were part of the landscape for centuries have thinned, congregations have left towns their families had been in for generations, and there are places on the map where the church that this article is describing is now a building with nobody in it. A frequency does not reverse any of that. It would be a cheat to write a triumphant essay about continuity and leave out what continuity has cost.

But that is exactly why it goes on the air rather than into an archive. A community that is dispersed is a community that can no longer count on the room — the compound, the hall, the annual feast where everybody was in one place. What it can still have is the same signal in every country it has been scattered into, playing the same song at the same hour to a family in Michigan and a family in Melbourne and a man early for a service in a Gulf car park. Broadcast is the one format that suits a scattered church, because it never required everybody to be in the same building.

So this frequency is not an outreach project in a difficult language, and it is not a gesture towards diversity on a dial. It is a station for a church that has been there the entire time, often at considerable cost, singing in the language it has always used, to people who do not need any of it explained.
All of which is history until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards, with further frequencies assigned and still in build behind the ones already on air.

So start at HM 328.70 — Inspire Crown. Start there whether or not you have a word of Arabic, and start there especially if the sentence Arabic worship music still sounds to you like a contradiction, because half an hour of it will do what the preceding paragraphs have been attempting and will do it faster. You will hear a language you have only ever heard in one register being used in another, by people to whom that is entirely unremarkable. And if you do have Arabic, you already know what this station is. It is the ordinary sound of a Friday morning, given a number that does not move.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an education. Put HM 328.70 on this afternoon while you are doing something else and leave it running for an hour, and do not look anything up while it plays. If somebody in the room asks what it is, tell them it is church music, which is true, and then say nothing further and let the rest of the hour make the point. That is how the correction has always travelled — not argued into anybody, simply playing in the background until it stops being surprising.
